governing_text: ParagraphPlan refines the document plan down to paragraphs: after the Brief, the Composer generates each Leg Waypoint's Paragraph Waypoints through the same kind of feedback loop as the Brief's, and hands them to the Packet through a planning record, never directly. Move information may be used up to Paragraph Waypoint generation and nowhere after it. It is not Reiter and Dale's microplanning: word choice, reference and sentence shape stay inside the one Writer call. [implemented-against: specs/spec-draft-pipeline/SPEC.md "The ParagraphPlan stage", copied 2026-10-14]
licensed_by: kogaki#1375 -- owner decision 2026-10-14: Paragraph Waypoint generation is its own stage after the Brief, named ParagraphPlan, with its own file and command; the ParagraphPlan file names the Brief it was made from and the Brief names nothing downstream; retries and limits follow the Brief's rules, `brief.call_limit_s` per call and `brief.unit_attempts` per unit, with no limit on the whole job.

judge.note: Every job unit of this stage is a headless session, a `claude -p` child that runs with no tools, spawned by the shared Detached Job supervisor (src/workflow/detached-job.mjs) with the binary the start act resolved. `model` NAMES THE BRIEF'S SETTING, `brief.judge_model`, because the owner decided this stage follows the Brief's rules rather than carrying settings of its own. `KOGAKI_JUDGE_CLI` replaces the resolved binary FOR FIXTURES ONLY.

job.note: ONE JOB UNIT PER LEG, in Reader Path order, and the two bounds are the Brief's own settings (kogaki#1375): a call running past `brief.call_limit_s` is stopped and spends one attempt, a refused answer spends one, an unreadable answer is asked again without spending one, and a unit that has spent `brief.unit_attempts` stops naming its Leg and the Waypoint its last refusal named. There is no limit on the whole job. Each attempt makes two calls: `paragraph_plan_unit` binds a paragraph Move to every Leg Waypoint and generates its Paragraph Waypoints, and `paragraph_plan_judge_unit` judges them against the bound Move. A refusal of either is put back into the next attempt's prompt verbatim.

paragraph_plan_unit.note: The first call of every attempt (kogaki#1375). It carries the second-pass judgment kogaki#1359 put inside the compose job, moved out of it: the Move binding is judged here, after the Brief is adopted, and its result never reaches the Brief. `src/paragraph-plan.mjs` renders this row through the shared `judgePrompt` renderer up to the input marker and appends one Leg's own input below it; `validateParagraphPlanUnit` reads the answer.
paragraph_plan_unit.judgment_point: plan the paragraphs of ONE Leg -- `leg_you_must_plan` in the input -- in two steps for EACH of its Leg Waypoints, in order. FIRST, bind ONE paragraph Move from `paragraph_moves_you_may_bind` (each Move's contract rides there from its record, its `before` and `after` -- maps keyed by dimension in the record -- rendered one `dimension: sentence` line per dimension, and its `segments` given as one entry per Segment: `segment`, its number; `does`, the step's operation, in prose; and `relation`, its relation to the Segment before it, in prose, empty on Segment 1): a Move fits where its `before` holds in the state the reader is in when this Leg Waypoint begins -- the Leg's `reader_state_before` for the first, and for every later one the state the previous Leg Waypoint's bound Move leaves the reader in -- and where its `after` moves the reader toward the NEXT Leg Waypoint's `point` (it rides on each entry as `next_point`), or toward the Leg's `reader_state_after` for the last. The next Leg Waypoint is fixed, so bind with it in view. Where NO Move in the library fits a Leg Waypoint, say so with `move: null` and one sentence `why` naming what no Move's `before` or `after` could hold -- never bind the nearest one. SECOND, for every Leg Waypoint whose Move you bound, generate the PARAGRAPH WAYPOINTS of the one paragraph carrying it: one Paragraph Waypoint per Segment of the bound Move's `segments`, in the Move's order, from three inputs and nothing else -- the Leg Waypoint's own `point`, the bound Move's `segments`, and `persona`, who the reader is and what they already know. A PARAGRAPH WAYPOINT IS A PART OF THE LEG WAYPOINT'S POINT: together, the Paragraph Waypoints of one Leg Waypoint say what its `point` says and nothing more. A Segment's `does` is an OPERATION TO PERFORM, NEVER A POINT TO STATE: it says what the paragraph does with its part at that place -- concede, define, name a case, answer -- and the Paragraph Waypoint for that Segment is the part of the Leg Waypoint's `point` on which that operation is performed, standing in the Segment's `relation` to the Paragraph Waypoint before it. The part's content comes from the Leg Waypoint's `point` alone; a `does` restated with the subject filled in is not a part of the point. A Paragraph Waypoint has the same shape as a Leg Waypoint: `point`, the proposition its paragraph makes, in the article's subject, in one sentence -- what the paragraph establishes, never how the reader is to feel, never a Segment's clause with the subject filled in, and never a sentence for the writer to copy -- and `serves`, the Strand ids of the Claims it serves, each one a Claim the parent Leg Waypoint serves; every Claim the parent serves is served by at least one of them. A Paragraph Waypoint that states what the paragraph is DOING to its reader -- announcing, defining rather than arguing, closing a list, leaving nothing open -- instead of a part of what the point says, is wrong, not merely stylistically off. Word choice, reference and sentence shape are NOT planned here; they stay with the Writer.
paragraph_plan_unit.input_shape: ONE plan record AT THE RECORD'S OWN ROOT -- `version` "1", the `leg_id` of the Leg in the input, and `waypoints`, one entry per Leg Waypoint in order: `{ "waypoint": <its 1-based number>, "move": <a Move id from the library, or null>, "why": <one sentence>, "paragraph_waypoints": [ { "point": <one sentence>, "serves": [<Strand id>, ...] }, ... ] }` -- `paragraph_waypoints` empty only where `move` is null
paragraph_plan_unit.refusal: a record naming another leg_id; `waypoints` not one entry per Leg Waypoint, or out of order; a key the record does not declare; a `move` naming no Move in the library; a `why` under four words; a Leg Waypoint whose Move is bound and which carries no Paragraph Waypoint; a Paragraph Waypoint with an empty point, an empty `serves`, a `serves` naming a Claim its parent Leg Waypoint does not serve, or any key but `point` and `serves`; a Claim the parent serves that no Paragraph Waypoint serves; a Paragraph Waypoint whose content is not recoverable from the Leg Waypoint's `point` -- stating what the paragraph does to its reader instead of a part of what the point says -- named by its number and why. `move: null` is a judgment, not malformed output: the unit is refused `no_paragraph_move_fits` naming the Leg and the Waypoint, and asked again with the sentence until `brief.unit_attempts` is spent. A BOUND MOVE THAT DOES NOT FILL A ROLE THIS STAGE NEEDS (`before`, `after`, `segments` or `breaks`) is not a refusal of your answer: the stage stops, naming the Move and the role, and nothing is defaulted.
paragraph_plan_unit.governing: SPEC-draft-pipeline, the ParagraphPlan stage and the Move boundary; kogaki#1375

paragraph_plan_judge_unit.note: The second call of every attempt (kogaki#1375), run by the supervisor's judge phase once `validateParagraphPlanUnit` has passed the first call's record. `src/paragraph-plan.mjs` renders this row through `judgePrompt` up to the input marker; `paragraphPlanJudgePrompt` appends the Leg's input and `paragraphPlanJudgeVerdict` reads the answer. A `does-not-fit` on any Leg Waypoint is a refusal of the attempt, and its sentence is put into the next attempt's first call.
paragraph_plan_judge_unit.judgment_point: judge the Paragraph Waypoints of ONE Leg -- `leg_you_must_judge` in the input -- one verdict per Leg Waypoint, against the paragraph Move bound to it, whose `before`, `after`, `segments` and `breaks` ride on the entry from its record, `before` and `after` rendered one `dimension: sentence` line per dimension: the Leg judge's own four things (kogaki#1378, owner decision 2026-10-14), plus two more. FIRST, whether the Paragraph Waypoints, read in order, begin from a state the Move's `before` holds -- the Leg's `reader_state_before` for the first Leg Waypoint, the state the previous one's Move leaves the reader in for every later one. SECOND, whether they end where the Move's `after` leaves the reader, moving toward the entry's `next_point` (the Leg's `reader_state_after` for the last). THIRD, whether, read in order, they follow the Move's order as its `segments` give it, one Paragraph Waypoint per Segment (kogaki#1412). FOURTH, whether they survive each test in the Move's `breaks`. FIFTH, whether each Paragraph Waypoint's content is recoverable from the Leg Waypoint's own `point` -- a Paragraph Waypoint is a part of that `point`, and a Segment's `does` is an operation performed on that part, never what it says; a Paragraph Waypoint that instead states what the paragraph does to its reader (announcing, defining rather than arguing, closing a list, leaving nothing open), or restates a Segment's `does` with the subject filled in, does not fit, however well it tracks the Segment. SIXTH, each Paragraph Waypoint against ITS OWN Segment -- the Nth Paragraph Waypoint against the Move's Nth Segment: whether it is a part on which that Segment's `does` can be performed, and whether it stands to the Paragraph Waypoint before it in that Segment's `relation`; a Paragraph Waypoint that neither performs its Segment's `does` nor sits in its `relation` -- a first point unrelated to Segment 1's `does`, as on the 2026-10-16 run, where Segment 1 conceded the distinction was hard and promised to simplify it and the first point stated an unrelated fact -- does not fit, however true it is of the Leg Waypoint's `point`. Where the Move carries no `segments`, SIXTH holds by default. Verdict `fits` only where all six hold, `does-not-fit` where any does not, with one sentence `why` naming the Paragraph Waypoint and the criterion it fails. Judge the points, not the Claims; how many Paragraph Waypoints there are is not judged.
paragraph_plan_judge_unit.input_shape: ONE verdict record AT THE RECORD'S OWN ROOT -- `version` "1", the `leg_id` of the Leg in the input, and `verdicts`, one per Leg Waypoint in order: `{ "waypoint": <its 1-based number>, "verdict": "fits" | "does-not-fit", "why": <one sentence> }`
paragraph_plan_judge_unit.refusal: a record carrying no `verdicts` array, or naming another leg_id; a verdict outside the closed set; a Leg Waypoint carrying no verdict, or two, or verdicts out of order; a `why` under four words -- each of these is this judge's own malformed output, and the same prompt is asked again. `does-not-fit` is a verdict, not malformed output: the attempt is refused with it and the plan is generated again.
